🔥Houthis wreak havoc on Saudi-backed mercs along the entire front
Saudi Arabia’s July 13 attack on Sanaa International Airport is proving a catastrophically costly mistake, not only boomeranging into direct [counterstrikes on the kingdom’s energy infrastructure](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74240) and [shutting down its Red Sea oil exports](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74250), but threatening to culminate in the total collapse of its Yemeni puppet state.
From the northeast to the southwest across a front stretching hundreds of kilometers, fierce battles are underway across nearly a dozen areas in the provinces of Al-Jawf, Marib, Al-Bayda, Ad-Dhale, Al-Hudaydah and Taiz.
🔴 In Taiz, Houthi forces have been attacking the massive Khalid bin Walid garrison overlooking Mokha Port – a vital chokepoint for Saudi puppet government supplies. Regional media reported Wednesday that the Houthis had captured the garrison
🔴 The Houthi media office posted footage of its warriors’ attacks on merc pickups and MRAPs, captured and killed enemy troops, and the wreckage of downed enemy drones in Al-Jawf
🔴 In Saudi Arabia proper, the Houthis launched fresh attacks targeting Aramco sites
🔴 Houthi Yemeni Armed Forces spokesman Yahya Saree reported Wednesday that Saudi warplanes had carried out over fifty airstrikes in a 12-hour period in the provinces of Al-Jawf, Marib, Taiz, Al-Hodeidah, Saada and Al-Bayda. These attacks will not go unanswered and unpunished, he warned
👉The fighting is by far the biggest escalation in Yemen since the 2022 ceasefire. Time is on the Houthis’ side, with the fighters controlling a majority of the country’s population centers, and deeply entrenched in mountain hideouts impenetrable even to attacks by hostile superpowers. They also enjoy military near-self-sufficiency and innovation, and tolerances for attrition far higher than their soft, moneyed Gulf enemies [thanks to their faith](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/66077).
The Houthis’ direct tribal ancestors have kept Yemen a graveyard of empires since at least 26 BC. The Saudis and their Gulf allies had better get in line if they want to join the list.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇵🇰🤔Pakistan's warning to the Houthis: rhetoric or readiness?
Following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia — including a major oil refinery that injured 73 people — Pakistan's Defense Minister Khawaja Asif stated that the Mecca Defense Pact (Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey) would be activated if the conflict spills over into Saudi territory. The pact treats an attack on one as an attack on all.
But is Pakistan truly prepared for military confrontation with the Houthis?
⚔️ Arguments for intervention
Decades of strategic ties bind Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. Asif noted that Pakistan already assisted Riyadh during the early stages of the Yemen conflict in 2014. Some reports even suggest that Islamabad has considered limited airstrikes against Houthi positions under the pact's framework.
👁 Arguments against intervention
However, significant obstacles remain. Pakistan's navy lacks power-projection capabilities in the Red Sea, being geared primarily toward coastal defense. Direct conflict with Iran-backed Houthis would endanger Pakistan's delicate relationship with Tehran. Domestically, parliament has historically opposed deeper involvement in Yemen, and a military escalation could fuel internal political instability.
🛡The most likely scenario: defense, not offense
Pakistan's response would likely focus on protecting Saudi territory rather than launching offensive operations. Asif himself stressed that the pact is defensive in nature. 
Expected measures include:
🌏Bolstering air defenses (Pakistan already has HQ-9 systems, JF-17 jets, and drones in the kingdom)
🌏Expanding the existing military contingent (media reports cite 8,000 troops, with potential for further increase) to serve as advisors or border guards
💬 Deterrence first
Pakistan's leadership ultimately prioritizes deterrence over direct engagement. Asif explicitly stated that the three allies "should not respond with aggression to aggression," expressing hope that the alliance's combined military weight alone would dissuade the Houthis.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

🇸🇾🇹🇷🇮🇱 Syria's security turns into Turkey-Israel tug of war
A rare high-level meeting between Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Mossad chief Roman Gofman opened a direct channel between Damascus and Tel Aviv — but also exposed a deeper problem: Syria is caught between two competing powers.
Days before the meeting, Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur Air Base in northwestern Syria, hammering runways and hangars. Damascus insisted the facility was simply being repaired, not prepared for Turkish forces. Israel saw any potential Turkish military presence there as a red line — and bombed it anyway.
Three realities on the ground:
🔴 Turkey wields significant influence in post-Assad Syria — politically and militarily
🔴 Israel enforces its red lines with strikes and incursions, refusing to limit its freedom of action in southern Syria
🔴 Syria is caught in the middle — negotiating with both, but unable to satisfy either without triggering the other
 
💬 "Syria's political decision rests in Ankara because Damascus cannot escape Turkish influence, while the security decision rests in Tel Aviv. If those limits are crossed, bombing becomes the answer," a Syrian official told the Cradle. 
The Sharaa government says it has already accepted many Israeli security demands and that a written framework was reached through US-mediated talks. Israel, however, continues to reject restrictions on its military freedom of action and refuses to treat the territory it controls in southern Syria as negotiable.

🇺🇸 The US confirms loss of advanced underwater drone to Iran—then rushes to downplay it
The US has confirmed that Iran captured an advanced American Dive-LD underwater drone—but was quick to add that the vehicle was “essentially dead in the water” before Tehran got its hands on it.
The drone “malfunctioned more than a day” before Iran captured it, CENTCOM spokesperson Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins argued.
👉 Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Navy earlier touted a complex intelligence operation to capture the 2.7-ton Dive-LD, designed for reconnaissance and mine-countermeasure missions, near the Strait of Hormuz.
IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi stressed that the seizure showed the strength of Iran’s surveillance capabilities in the strategic waterway. “Dominance over the Persian Gulf belongs to our young technology specialists,” he underscored.
For the US, Iran’s capture of an advanced American unmanned system is yet another awkward reminder that Tehran is proving far harder to intimidate — let alone defeat — than Washington likes to admit.
After months of costly military actions and growing pressure on US weapons stocks, the idea that Iran can simply be overwhelmed by American firepower looks increasingly questionable. Meanwhile, US forces have already burned through large portions of key missile inventories, with some estimates putting Patriot interceptor depletion at up to three-fifths and THAAD at around half. Replenishing some of these systems could take years.

events.text:
🤥 Lunar land grab: Trump's cosmic delusions & the very real race for the Moon
Not content with unleashing mayhem [on Earth,](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74247) US President Donald Trump, [in a signature deranged bluster](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73812), has declared the Moon US property on Truth Social. 
The absurd insinuation collides with the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 - ratified by over a hundred nations, including the US – stating that celestial bodies are not subject to national appropriation.
Yet Trump’s buffoonery should not be entirely dismissed - it mirrors an intensifying contest for lunar mineral wealth. 
Earth’s terrestrial resources are finite and the scramble for [critical minerals ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73579)and energy is reshaping geopolitics.
The US is already fuming that China has[ pulled ahead ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/56929)in the rare-earth mineral race, leaving the US far behind.
Specifically of interest is [the Moon’s South Pole](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/52602), with high ridges, near-permanent sunlight, and craters believed to hide water-ice deposits.
Those deposits could be potentially turned into drinking water, breathable air to sustain crews, or rocket fuel.
First infrastructure there could potentially mean lasting logistical and strategic dominance.
Under Trump, the US has been pushing an aggressive timeline per the executive order "Ensuring American Space Superiority”:
🔴 [ the delay-mired NASA plans ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70939)an Artemis III crewed lunar landing by 2028 and hopes for a permanent Moon outpost plus nuclear reactor by 2030+
🔴 it rallied 69 nations behind the Artemis Accords - its long-term [Moon colonization roadmap ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70135)
🔴 the private sector is muscling in, with Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos's Blue Origin building capabilities for potential resource extraction
🔴 [Blue Origin secured contracts](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70135) to help deliver infrastructure equipment to a future lunar settlement
🔴 US scramble comes hot on the heels of Russia and China, whose [International Lunar Research Station](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/53231) targets a crewed landing in the same decade, with thirteen nations already signed on 
🔴 [China’s](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/48829) Chang'e program has already been the first to land a rover on the Moon's far side, returning scientific sample
🔴 India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar South Pole in 2023 & plans a space station by 2035
In a legal sleight of hand, the US' 2015 Commercial Space Act granted American citizens the right to own, sell, and use space resources like water and minerals after extraction – a self-serving "carve-out" in effect gutting the 1967 treaty’s spirit.
